props.title: The Taste of Cherry

sections.content: The Taste of Cherry (1997) stands as Iranian master Abbas Kiarostami's most profound meditation on life and death. The film follows Mr. Badii, driving through Tehran's dusty outskirts, searching for someone to bury him after his planned suicide. Kiarostami's signature long takes and car conversations create an hypnotic rhythm, while challenging traditional narrative expectations. This approach influenced later minimalist works like Ten (2002) and Certified Copy (2010), establishing a style that merged documentary-like observation with philosophical depth.

sections.content: The film's contemplative power comes from its deceptive simplicity. Like fellow Iranian New Wave landmark A Moment of Innocence (1996) by Mohsen Makhmalbaf, it uses minimal elements to explore existential themes. The recurring image of Badii's Range Rover winding through barren landscapes echoes similar road imagery in Kiarostami's earlier And Life Goes On (1992), suggesting both physical and spiritual journeys.

Kiarostami's controversial ending - breaking the fourth wall with behind-the-scenes footage - prefigured similar meta-cinematic techniques in films like Adaptation (2002) and Synecdoche, New York (2008). This bold formal choice transforms the meditation on mortality into a reflection on cinema's relationship with reality, similar to how Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010) blends the metaphysical with the mundane. sections.content: The Taste of Cherry emerged during a crucial period for Iranian cinema, alongside works like The White Balloon (1995) and Children of Heaven (1997). These films used neorealist techniques and philosophical inquiry to bypass censorship while addressing profound human questions. Kiarostami's influence extends to contemporary Iranian filmmakers like Asghar Farhadi, whose About Elly (2009) continues this tradition of moral complexity within seemingly simple narratives.
